title: A new column needs an explicit landing policy
goal: Trace one arriving coupon_code column through Databricks Auto Loader and Snowflake COPY INTO, then choose pause, rescue, or controlled evolution.
concept:
A warehouse expects boxes with three labels: order_id, amount, and event_time. One morning a box also has coupon_code. The safe question is not simply “Can the system add it?” It is “Should this load pause for review, preserve the unexpected field separately, or change the table automatically?”

Schema evolution is a policy decision at the ingestion boundary. The data can be preserved while the published contract remains controlled.
example: File 1 has three columns. File 2 adds coupon_code=FALL10. A pause-and-restart path updates approved schema before File 2 continues. A rescue path keeps the current table columns and stores the extra field in a JSON rescue column. An automatic-evolution path adds a table column only when its required flags and privileges are present.

use_case.when: Use an explicit schema-drift policy for semi-structured or partner files whose columns can change independently of your pipeline release.
use_case.example: A retail partner adds coupon_code before your silver-table model is ready. Preserve the value, alert the owner, and expose it only after contract review.
use_case.decision: Pause and restart when every new column must be visible and reviewed. Rescue when continuity matters more than immediate promotion. Allow table evolution only for trusted file loads with naming, privilege, downstream-compatibility, and observability controls.

practice: Choose what happens to coupon_code. Watch the landing schema, rescue area, and operational state change independently.
boundary: The browser models one additive column. It does not run Databricks or Snowflake, infer data types, process nested fields, widen types, model case rules, partition columns, CSV parsing, NOT NULL changes, Snowpipe, checkpoint recovery, downstream contracts, or cost. Vendor SQL/PySpark is sourced but unexecuted.

';};schemaPolicy.onchange=paintSchema;paintSchema();

Preserve it in a rescue/quarantine field and alert
Rescue keeps the data without silently changing the consumer contract.
What does schema evolution not remove?
The need to test downstream compatibility and privileges
Automatic mechanics do not approve a contract change.
Why might a deliberate restart be useful?
It creates an observable review point before the new schema continues
A fail/restart boundary can turn drift into an explicit operational event.

product_sections.title: Databricks: fail-and-restart or rescue deliberately
product_sections.html:
Mechanism. With Auto Loader and addNewColumns, discovery of a new column updates schema information and the stream initially fails; after restart it uses the evolved schema. With rescue, the schema does not evolve and unexpected fields land in _rescued_data.

# sourced PySpark; not executed here(spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", schema_path) .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "rescue") .load(source_path))

Failure/fix. addNewColumns without restart handling stops at the drift boundary. Configure Jobs retry/restart and alerting, or choose rescue when a stable landing schema is required.

Limits. Supplying a fixed schema changes supported modes; use schema hints for known types. Existing column types do not automatically evolve in the same way. This local model made no Databricks call.
product_sections.markdown: Auto Loader addNewColumns first fails when a new column appears, then continues with the evolved schema after restart. Rescue keeps the schema fixed and records unexpected fields in _rescued_data. PySpark is sourced and unexecuted.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: COPY evolves only when all gates are open
product_sections.html:
Mechanism. File-load schema evolution requires the table flag, MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME, and a loading role with EVOLVE SCHEMA or ownership. It applies to COPY INTO and Snowpipe file loads, not ordinary INSERT.

-- sourced SQL; not executed hereALTER TABLE raw_orders  SET ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE;COPY INTO raw_orders FROM @orders_stage  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = PARQUET)  MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE;

Failure/fix. Missing any gate means the table does not evolve as intended. Provision the narrow privilege, enable the table deliberately, and test file-format rules.

Limits. Evolution can add columns and can drop NOT NULL from columns absent in new files. CSV has additional PARSE_HEADER/count-mismatch requirements. This local model made no Snowflake call.
product_sections.markdown: Snowflake automatic file-load evolution needs ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION, MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME, and EVOLVE SCHEMA or OWNERSHIP. It is limited to COPY INTO and Snowpipe. SQL is sourced and unexecuted.

title: The work failure stays primary; close failures become suppressed
goal: Use Java try-with-resources so cleanup runs without hiding the exception that caused the operation to fail.
concept:
Imagine a delivery truck crashes, and then its broken door jams while responders unload it. The crash explains why the delivery failed; the jam is also important, but it should not replace the original cause.

Java try-with-resources closes every initialized AutoCloseable. If the body and close() both throw, the body exception is propagated and the close exception is attached as suppressed.
example: A JDBC transaction throws "insert failed". Closing the connection also throws "socket close failed". Logs should show the insert failure as primary and the socket failure in getSuppressed(). A hand-written finally block that simply throws from close can mask the real cause.

use_case.when: Use try-with-resources for files, streams, JDBC connections/statements/result sets, and other AutoCloseable resources.
use_case.example: An order insert fails and the database connection also errors during close; incident responders need both failures in causal order.
use_case.decision: Let try-with-resources establish primary/suppressed ordering. Log suppressed failures, and design close methods to be idempotent and specific. Do not ignore cleanup failures that may signal leaks or incomplete flushes.

practice: Toggle whether the body and close fail. The stack shows which failure is primary and which is preserved underneath it.
boundary: The browser models one resource. Real Java closes multiple resources in reverse declaration order and can suppress multiple failures. It does not model Errors, initialization failure, logging frameworks, JDBC rollback, async cleanup, or process termination. The Java replay was executed during the build.

'+(b?'Suppressed':'Primary')+'

';failureWorld.innerHTML=h+'
';};bodyFails.onchange=paintFailure;closeFails.onchange=paintFailure;paintFailure();
questions: The try body and close both throw. Which is propagated?
The body exception, with close attached as suppressed
Try-with-resources preserves the work failure as the primary cause.
Where do you find the close failure?
Suppressed exceptions preserve sibling cleanup failures.
Why prefer this over a naive finally close?
A close failure will not mask the earlier work failure

steps.code: class LoudResource implements AutoCloseable { public void close() { throw new RuntimeException("close failed"); } }
steps.note: Define a resource whose close operation fails.
Prepare to capture the propagated exception.

steps.code: try (LoudResource r = new LoudResource()) { throw new RuntimeException("work failed"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { primary = e; suppressed = e.getSuppressed().length; }

title: An ADR is evidence, not a forever rule
goal: Record the assumption behind an architecture decision and supersede the ADR when that assumption stops being true.
concept:
A bridge sign says “safe for 10-ton trucks.” If the fleet moves to 20-ton trucks, the sign did not become false because it was poorly written; its operating assumption expired.

An architecture decision record should preserve context, options, decision, consequences, status, owner, and change history. A later decision does not erase the old one; it marks it superseded and links the replacement.
example: ADR-042 chooses one shared Kafka cluster because peak load is under 50 MB/s and tenant isolation is logical. Six months later one tenant reaches 45 MB/s alone. The team does not silently edit history. ADR-087 records the changed assumption, chooses cells, and marks ADR-042 superseded.

use_case.when: Create an ADR for choices that shape structure, non-functional requirements, dependencies, interfaces, or construction technique.
use_case.example: Choose shared versus cell-based Kafka infrastructure, with an explicit revisit trigger when a tenant exceeds 30% of cluster capacity.
use_case.decision: Keep the original record immutable enough to explain history. Add measurable assumptions and triggers, assign an owner, and supersede rather than delete when the context changes.

practice: Move observed tenant load past the recorded assumption. Watch the decision change from valid to revisit to superseded.
boundary: The browser evaluates one numeric assumption. Real decisions have multiple uncertain assumptions, qualitative consequences, stakeholder tradeoffs, irreversible costs, and review cadence. It does not approve an architecture.

';};tenantShare.oninput=paintAdr;replacementWritten.onchange=paintAdr;paintAdr();

Reopen the decision with current evidence
The changed context is decision input.
Why keep the old ADR after replacement?
It preserves why the old system made sense and what changed
It proves the owner was wrong
Decision history prevents circular debate and supports learning.
Minimum useful ADR content includes what?
Context, decision, consequences, status, owner/change history
A decision without context and consequences is hard to evaluate later.

title: Choose whether a tool failure becomes context or stops the run
goal: Use failure_error_function to return an approved model-visible error—or set it to None when the harness must fail fast.
concept:
A restaurant waiter can tell the guest “the kitchen is out of salmon; choose again,” or can close the restaurant because the freezer alarm indicates unsafe food. Both are failures, but only one should become a recoverable conversation.

OpenAI Agents SDK function tools can turn a tool exception into a model-visible string. The default is generic and does not expose the exception. A custom handler can return approved details. Passing None propagates the exception instead.
example: A catalog lookup times out. The tool returns {code: TEMPORARY, retry_after_s: 5}; the agent may retry once or ask the user. A policy-evaluation tool fails closed: its exception propagates and the run stops, because asking the model to improvise would weaken authorization.

use_case.when: Use model-visible failures for bounded, recoverable outcomes the model can safely act on. Use fail-fast for invariant violations, authorization uncertainty, corrupted state, and failures requiring operator intervention.
use_case.example: A metadata search timeout is recoverable; inability to verify a production-deploy approval is not.
use_case.decision: Classify errors before exposing them, return only application-approved details, bound retries, and trace the original exception privately. Never place secrets, stack traces, tokens, or internal topology in model-visible text.

practice: Select the failure class and policy. The visual shows whether the model receives a safe recovery instruction or the harness terminates.
boundary: The browser is a policy table, not the Agents SDK. It does not execute tools, retries, callbacks, MCP servers, approvals, tracing, timeouts, cancellation, or nested agents. The Python replay is a local policy example.

title: Squeeze one uncertainty to protect a cat qubit from bit flips
goal: Understand the reported 160× bit-flip-time improvement, why squeezing helps, and why this is not a complete fault-tolerant computer.
concept:
Squeezing a balloon makes it narrower in one direction and wider in another. Quantum squeezing similarly redistributes uncertainty between paired variables; it does not remove uncertainty.

A cat qubit stores logical information in separated oscillator states. The environment can effectively “measure” a noise-sensitive direction and cause errors. The paper deforms the cat state with squeezing so that environmental measurement is weaker along that direction.
example: The researchers report a squeezed cat qubit with a 22-second bit-flip time at a 1.3-microsecond phase-flip time and mean photon number 4.1—160× the standard cat comparison. The key claim is selective protection: much longer bit-flip time with minimal phase-flip penalty.

use_case.when: Use this research when assessing hardware-biased quantum error correction and whether physical encoding can reduce one dominant error before higher-level codes handle the rest.
use_case.example: A quantum architecture team compares how many physical resources a multi-cat logical qubit needs when bit flips are suppressed at the device level.
use_case.decision: Treat 160× as a reported experimental comparison under stated conditions, not a universal constant. Examine phase flips, gates, fabrication, calibration, scaling, correlated errors, and full logical performance.

practice: Increase the synthetic squeeze factor. Watch the protected axis narrow and the teaching bit-flip time grow while the phase-flip boundary remains visible.
boundary: The ellipse and values are a qualitative teaching model except for the paper's reported 22 s, 1.3 μs, mean photon number 4.1, and 160× comparison. It does not simulate a harmonic oscillator, Wigner function, decoherence, gates, tomography, error correction thresholds, uncertainty relations, or a quantum processor.

protected width '+(1/(1+s/5)).toFixed(2)+'
teaching flip time '+improvement+'×

Research anchor: the experiment reports 160× under its measured conditions; this slider is not its fit.

title: A failed step silently adds success() to the next condition
goal: Make cleanup and diagnostics run under the intended status without creating cancellation-resistant jobs.
concept:
A fire alarm closes an office. A normal delivery rule—“if it is after 5 PM, lock the archive”—still assumes the office is operating normally. To override that assumption, the rule must explicitly say what to do during an alarm.

GitHub Actions applies a default success() status check to an if that contains no status function. After a failed step, if: steps.test.outcome == 'failure' alone can still be skipped; include failure().
example: Tests fail. An upload step with no if is skipped. if: failure() uploads failure diagnostics. always() also runs on cancellation and is suited to small step-level logging, but GitHub warns against using it for critical tasks that might hang. !cancelled() runs after success or failure but stops on cancellation.

use_case.when: Use status functions for diagnostic uploads, cleanup, notifications, and dependent jobs whose behavior differs after failure or cancellation.
use_case.example: Upload test reports after a test failure, but do not start a long source checkout after the workflow has been canceled.
use_case.decision: Use failure() for failure-only evidence, always() sparingly for short cancellation-safe steps, and !cancelled() for work that should run after success/failure but honor cancellation.

practice: Select an upstream result and condition. The job timeline shows whether the diagnostic step runs.
boundary: The browser evaluates four simplified status choices. GitHub expressions also include ancestor job status, continue-on-error outcome versus conclusion, matrices, skipped jobs, cancellation timing, and runner termination. No workflow ran.

tests
'+s+'
diagnostic upload
'+(run?'runs':'skipped')+'

'+(c==='default'?'Implicit success() applies':c==='always'?'Runs even on cancellation; keep it bounded':'Explicit status policy')+'

';};testStatus.onchange=paintAction;uploadIf.onchange=paintAction;paintAction();

title: If-Match turns a stale write into 412, not a lost update
goal: Use strong ETags as optimistic concurrency tokens so two clients cannot silently overwrite each other.
concept:
Two people open the same shared document at version 7. Alice saves first, creating version 8. Bob's screen still shows version 7. If Bob saves without a version check, he can erase Alice's work.

An API can return a strong ETag: "v7". The client sends If-Match: "v7" with its PUT or PATCH. The origin server compares before applying the method. If the current tag is now "v8", it does not apply the stale write and can return 412 Precondition Failed.
example: Alice and Bob GET order 42 at v7. Alice changes the address with If-Match v7; the server writes and returns v8. Bob changes the delivery date with If-Match v7; the comparison fails, so Bob must GET v8, reconcile, and submit a new change.

use_case.when: Use If-Match for editable resources where parallel clients can read and then update the same representation.
use_case.example: A customer and an operations agent edit different fields of the same order within seconds.
use_case.decision: Issue a strong validator that changes whenever relevant representation data changes. Require If-Match for unsafe updates, return 428 when the precondition is missing if that is your API policy, and return 412 for a stale validator.

practice: Step Alice and Bob through their writes. Change whether Bob refreshes before retrying and watch the stored version.
boundary: The browser uses integer versions as ETags. Real validators are opaque, strong versus weak comparison matters, representations can vary, a 2xx may be allowed when the requested change is already applied, and PATCH merge semantics remain application-specific. No HTTP request ran.

'+(refresh?'Bob reconciled before writing':'Alice's change remains safe; Bob must refresh')+'

';};bobRefresh.onchange=paintHttp;paintHttp();
